newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Dollar closes weaker in Asia, eyes on U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes weaker in Asia, eyes on U.S. data.

text.p: The U.S. dollar ended a sluggish Asian session slightly weaker against the New York close, but dealers said trade would remain thin throughout the early part of the European session.
"It's been dead, very quiet indeed," one analyst said.
Dollar/yen was trapped in a tight range, caught between Japanese orders at 126.40/50 and 127.00/10.
The 127.10 level is being aggressively defended by an Asian player with a big position that expires on May 1, the analyst said. But one Singapore dealer was sceptical.
"The whole world is talking about a knock-out option in dollar/yen at 127.30. I doubt there is any and if so, maybe it's only $100-200 (million) worth," he said.
He said huge stop-loss buy orders were building above 1.7425 marks and 127.40/50 yen. "There's a big risk we'll have a 50 points gap up if we break these levels," he said.
Dollar/mark tried but failed to break 1.7300 when London opened and has settled back to trade thinly at earlier levels.
Attention was now focussed on the release of the U.S. first quarter employment cost index at 1230 GMT.

An increase of 0.9 percent is expected to prompt weakness in U.S. treasuries but the U.S. dollar will remain well-supported unless inflation fears prompt a widespread sell-off in bonds, the analyst said.
Singapore dealers said the dollar showed a strong undertone but players were reluctant to buy it aggressively after the G7's renewed call for stability in foreign exchange markets.
"It's just the authorities' game to keep the market a little bit uncertain. As long as they're uncertain, they won't overbuy the dollar," a European bank dealer said, citing the G7 communique.

He said the dollar still showed upward momentum but players would be cautious of pushing it up too fast, particularly as any central bank intervention would be more effective in markets thinned by the absence of Tokyo players.
With Tokyo closed for the Golden Week holiday, activity was expected to remain light until Monday with most attention focussed on sterling and the May 1 election in Britain.
A slew of U.S. economic data could also generate interest.
